Walking is simple and free. It is a simple way to get more active and feel better. Many people start walking, then stop, because a plain walk feels dull. Music can change that. An album keeps your mind on track. Your mind stays with the music, and your feet keep moving. This guide shows how to pair a walk with a full album.

## Why walking works

Walking is simple and free, and it helps you get more active. Brisk walking can help you build stamina, burn excess calories and make your heart healthier. A brisk 10-minute daily walk has lots of health benefits and counts towards your 150 minutes of weekly exercise. This advice is for adults aged 19 to 64. Comfortable shoes are all you need to start. Walking to the shops or to work counts too. Try the stairs in place of the lift.

A brisk walk is about 3 miles an hour, which is faster than a stroll. You can tell you are walking briskly if you can still talk but cannot sing the words to a song. Walk so you can still talk, but not sing. If you cannot talk, slow down a little. If singing feels easy, walk a bit faster.

## Music takes your mind off the effort

Walking while listening to music can take your mind off the effort. It can also get you into a rhythm and help you walk faster. Music can get you into a rhythm. You will be surprised at how fast the time goes when you are walking to your favourite tunes.

In one study, people walk faster on music than on metronome stimuli. The music tempi in that study varied between 50 and 190 beats per minute. Fast music at 140 beats per minute promotes a higher rating of perceived exertion and greater performance in walking. The study tested 28 adult women between 29 and 51 years old. The women walked for 30 minutes in the test. The test compared no music, music at 90 beats per minute, and music at 140 beats per minute. Music at 90 beats per minute is slow, and music at 140 beats per minute is fast. In the study, the women walked at their own pace while the music played.

## Why a full album, not a shuffle

An album is more than a set of songs. Listening to a full album lets you hear how the songs fit as one work. The order is part of the work. A first song opens a door, and the songs that follow build on it. A slow song sounds new after a fast one. An interlude can clean the ear before a big song.

Shuffle breaks the order and builds a mix built on surprise. To hear the order as the artist made it, listen to the album in order. Listen to it in order, without looking at your phone for the first three songs. Listen twice to learn the shape of the work. The first time, just go along with it. The second time, note where the energy shifts and which song acts as a door. Attention is trained through curiosity, not rigidity.

## Pick the right pace

A brisk walk is about 3 miles an hour. A steady beat sets the pace for your feet. Try a slow tempo first, then try a faster one, and see which pace feels right for you. Fast music can push your pace up, so pick a tempo that fits the walk you want. A calm album fits a slow walk, and a bright album fits a brisk walk. Your pace should feel steady, not rushed.

## A simple plan for your first week

Pick one album you like. Play it from the first song to the last. Start with a 10-minute walk each day. Keep your phone in your pocket for the first three songs. Walk in the order of the songs, and let each song set your pace. When a song ends, keep walking and let the next song start. If you feel tired, slow down and walk at a pace that feels easy. Note one change in the music each day. A walk with a friend can make the time pass fast. After a week, try a new album and see how it feels.

## Stay safe while you listen

Keep the volume low so you can still hear the world around you. Look up, not down, most of all near curbs, stairs, and crossings. Cross the street only at crosswalks, stop signs, or traffic lights. If you need to make a call or send a text, stop walking and step out of the flow of traffic. Wear light shoes with a good grip. Take water on long walks, most of all on hot days. Tell a friend your route when you walk alone at night.
